questions_asked: On Amazon, are most customers who buy a product silent, with only a few leaving a star rating or a written review? Roughly what fraction actually rate or review?
Among the people who do leave ratings and reviews, is the average star rating you would expect from them lower, higher, or about the same as the true average satisfaction of all buyers? Why?
When judging whether a newly launched product is trending up or down from its first months of ratings and reviews, what single change would a marketing manager most trust as a warning sign?
expert_answers:
Yes — the large majority of Amazon purchasers leave no rating or review at all. The commonly cited empirical regularity is that only on the order of 1–5% of buyers ever post a star rating, and written reviews are a subset of that (roughly 1–3% of buyers, often lower). So for every 100 purchasers, expect only a handful of ratings and fewer still with text.

This is an empirical judgment, not a precise figure; it varies by category, price, and product age. Higher-priced, higher-consideration items (e.g., microwaves) tend to draw somewhat higher review rates than cheap, low-involvement items (e.g., pacifiers), and dissatisfied customers are disproportionately more likely to write than satisfied ones. But the core point holds: reviewers are a small, self-selected minority, so review data are not a representative sample of all buyers.

Higher than the true average satisfaction of all buyers.

The reason is selection: the people who bother to rate are not a random sample. On Amazon, the dominant driver of posting is strong positive feeling — buyers who are delighted often want to reward the product and the seller, and there is mild social pressure to leave a rating after a good experience. Dissatisfied buyers are also over-represented relative to their share, but the net effect on the *mean* is usually upward, because the mass of mildly-satisfied silent buyers (who would rate 3–4) is missing, while enthusiastic 5-star raters are disproportionately present.

So the observed average star rating tends to sit above the true mean satisfaction of the full buyer population. This is an empirical regularity, not a precise offset; the gap is larger for cheap, low-involvement items and smaller where dissatisfaction drives posting (e.g., defective or misleading products).

A sustained drop in the **average star rating** over successive months — specifically, a decline that persists across several consecutive months rather than a one-month dip — is the single change a marketing manager would most trust as a warning sign.

Why this one: it is the most direct, least noisy signal of deteriorating satisfaction, and it is robust to the fact that review volume is small and self-selected. A falling average means the mix of new raters is shifting toward lower satisfaction, which is the thing that actually erodes future sales.

Caveats that make it trustworthy only when sustained: early months have few reviews, so single-month swings are mostly noise; and a rating drop accompanied by rising review volume is a stronger warning than a drop on flat volume, because it suggests the decline is real and being noticed.
